description: Willmott and Young's symmetrical family, stratified diffusion, and contemporary family issues.
content_html:
How Have Families Changed Over Time?

Sociologists examine how family relationships have changed across three broad historical periods: pre-industrial, industrial and contemporary. Understanding this historical trajectory — and the competing perspectives on whether change has been progressive or problematic — is central to the families topic. Different perspectives offer strikingly different evaluations of the same changes.

The Pre-Industrial Family

In pre-industrial Britain (before approximately the mid-eighteenth century), the family was primarily a unit of economic production. Most families worked together in agriculture or craft production. The household typically included not just parents and children but also servants, apprentices and extended kin. The boundary between work and home was blurred; family members of all ages contributed economically. Peter Laslett’s historical research challenged the idea that the pre-industrial family was predominantly an extended unit, finding that nuclear family households were more common than often assumed. However, extended kinship networks of support remained significant even if not co-resident.

The Industrial Family

Industrialisation (roughly 1750–1900) transformed the family. Paid work moved out of the home and into factories and offices. This created a sharper separation between the public sphere (paid work) and the private sphere (the home). The nuclear family became the dominant household form, with a clear gender division: the man in paid employment, the woman managing the home. Working-class families often had both adults and children in paid work in early industrialisation, but as the nineteenth century progressed, middle-class values of the male breadwinner and the “domestic wife” spread downward through the principle of stratified diffusion. The family shifted from a unit of production to a unit of consumption.

Willmott and Young: Towards the Symmetrical Family

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) developed an influential account of the contemporary family in their study The Symmetrical Family. They argued that the family had passed through three historical stages and was now entering a fourth, characterised by the symmetrical family. In this form, both partners are likely to be in paid employment, both participate in domestic tasks and child rearing, and both have leisure time together. Willmott and Young saw this as a positive “march of progress.”

Central to their explanation was the principle of stratified diffusion. They observed that the symmetrical family pattern appeared first among middle-class households and was gradually spreading to the working class as material conditions improved. Higher incomes, better housing and the growth of home-centred leisure (television, home ownership) all contributed to what Willmott and Young called privatised instrumentalism — families becoming increasingly self-contained and home-focused.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that the family was becoming “symmetrical” — roles more equally shared — and that this change spread from middle-class to working-class families through the principle of stratified diffusion. They presented this as a positive historical progression.

Ann Oakley challenged Willmott and Young directly, arguing that the “march of progress” narrative was misleading. Her research found that the domestic division of labour remained highly unequal: women still performed the vast majority of domestic tasks and child care, even when in full-time paid employment. Oakley criticised the low threshold used by Willmott and Young to define male domestic participation. From her feminist perspective, the symmetrical family was a myth that served to obscure continuing gender inequality in the home.

From a Marxist perspective, the “march of progress” in family life is better understood as a change in the form of family serving capitalism rather than as genuine liberation. Higher wages and consumerism drew the working-class family into the home-centred, high-consumption lifestyle that generates profit for the bourgeoisie. Privatised instrumentalism, far from representing freedom, ties families more closely to consumption patterns that benefit capitalism.

Contemporary Family Issues

The spec identifies several contemporary family issues that sociologists study. These reflect the ways in which family relationships continue to evolve and the challenges that arise from changing social conditions:

  • Quality of parenting: sociologists debate whether parenting standards are changing. Some argue that greater awareness of child development and increased investment of time and resources in children has improved parenting; others point to the pressures of long working hours, poverty and social media as creating new challenges. Perspectives differ on what “good parenting” means and who defines it.
  • Relationships between teenagers and adults: the concept of adolescence as a distinct life stage is itself a modern, socially constructed category. Sociologists note that the extension of education and financial dependence on parents has prolonged adolescence. Intergenerational tensions within families are studied as social phenomena rather than as natural or inevitable.
  • Care of disabled and elderly family members: as life expectancy has increased, the issue of who cares for elderly or disabled family members has grown. Feminist sociologists note that caring responsibilities fall disproportionately on women. The state provides some care services, but much informal care is provided by female relatives.
  • Arranged marriage: sociologists distinguish between arranged marriage (where families identify suitable partners but individuals give their consent) and forced marriage (where individuals are compelled to marry against their will, which is illegal in the UK). Arranged marriage is practised in various communities in the UK and globally and is not inherently coercive; sociologists study it without imposing a single moral judgement.
Key Fact

The spec requires knowledge of contemporary family issues including quality of parenting, teenager–adult relationships, care of the disabled and elderly, and arranged marriage. Sociologists study each of these as social phenomena shaped by wider structural factors — not as simply individual or natural.

From a functionalist perspective, changes in family relationships across history represent the family adapting to meet the changing needs of society. As the economy shifted from agriculture to industry to post-industrial service work, the family shed functions it could no longer efficiently perform (transferred to schools, hospitals and the state) and retained those it was best placed to deliver — primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Willmott and Young’s symmetrical family thesis can be read as a functionalist account: the family evolves to meet the needs of a more egalitarian society. Critics of the functionalist view, however, argue that it presents change as evolutionary and benign while obscuring the structural inequalities that shape family life.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question about Willmott and Young, name them directly and describe both their key concept (the symmetrical family) and their explanation of how change occurs (the principle of stratified diffusion). A common mistake is describing the symmetrical family without explaining the mechanism — you need both for 4 marks. On the 12-mark Discuss, a strong response on changing family relationships must present the “march of progress” argument (Willmott and Young) alongside its critics (Oakley’s feminist critique; Marxist critique) and reach a supported judgement. Avoid treating Willmott and Young’s thesis as fact — present it as one perspective and then evaluate it using Oakley’s counter-evidence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Families have changed across three historical periods: pre-industrial (family as unit of production), industrial (separation of work and home, male breadwinner/female homemaker), and contemporary (growth of dual career families, greater role sharing, privatisation of family life).
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the modern family was becoming symmetrical, with roles more equally shared, driven by the principle of stratified diffusion from middle to working class. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed women still performed the majority of domestic labour.
  • Contemporary family issues studied by sociologists include quality of parenting, teenager–adult relationships, care of disabled and elderly family members, and arranged marriage. Each is shaped by structural factors including gender, class, ethnicity and state policy.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologists developed the concept of the 'symmetrical family' and the 'principle of stratified diffusion' to explain changes in family relationships?
A) Parsons and Murdock
B) Willmott and Young
C) Oakley and Zaretsky
D) Delphy and Leonard
Define the term 'adolescence' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying adolescence as a stage between childhood and adulthood; 1 mark for noting that it is socially constructed — its length and characteristics are shaped by social and historical factors (such as the extension of compulsory education) rather than being purely biological. Example: 'Adolescence is a socially constructed stage of life between childhood and adulthood, characterised by physical maturation and changing social expectations; its meaning and duration vary across societies and historical periods.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one contemporary family issue that sociologists study.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an issue from the spec list (quality of parenting, relationships between teenagers and adults, care of the disabled or elderly, arranged marriage). 2 marks for a developed description that explains why it is sociologically significant: e.g. 'Feminist sociologists note that care of elderly family members falls disproportionately on women. As life expectancy has increased, the question of who provides informal care has grown in significance, with caring responsibilities adding to women's domestic burden alongside paid work.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ideas of Willmott and Young on changing relationships within families.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Willmott and Young. 1 mark for describing the symmetrical family (roles more equally shared; both partners in paid employment and sharing domestic tasks). 1 mark for the principle of stratified diffusion (change begins among the middle class and spreads to the working class). 1 mark for a developed explanation or contextual detail: e.g. they described a 'march of progress' in which higher incomes, home ownership and privatised home-centred leisure contributed to the growth of the symmetrical family, first among professional families and later among working-class households.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the role of the family changed from the pre-industrial to the industrial period.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the pre-industrial family as primarily a unit of economic production (family members worked together in agriculture or craft production). 1 mark for identifying the industrial family as a unit of consumption (paid work moved to factories and offices, creating a separation between public and private spheres). 1 mark for a developed point: e.g. industrialisation created a sharper gender division — the man in paid employment, the woman in the home — reflecting the growing influence of middle-class breadwinner norms. 1 mark for a further detail or example: e.g. the extension of the male breadwinner/domestic wife model to the working class occurred through stratified diffusion as wages rose and middle-class family values spread.

practice_questions.text: "Family relationships in Britain have improved for all family members over time." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument. Arguments in support: Willmott and Young's 'march of progress' — symmetrical family, greater gender equality, privatised home-centred family life; growth of dual career families; longer life expectancy; better legal protections for children (Children Act 1989) and same-sex partners. Arguments against: Oakley's feminist critique — domestic labour remains unequal; women perform the double shift; feminist sociologists question whether change has benefited women. Marxist critique — privatisation of family life serves capitalism; increased consumption tied families to capitalist production; the improvement narrative conceals structural inequalities. New Right concern about family breakdown as negative change. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately. Supported conclusion weighing the evidence.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present, named sociologists, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Willmott and Young described the contemporary family as 'symmetrical'. What does this mean?
options: Both partners have exactly equal amounts of free time
The husband and wife each specialise in one area of family life
Partners share domestic tasks and leisure relatively equally, though not identically
The family is geographically separated across generations

knowledge_checks.q: Which perspective argues that changes to family life represent a 'march of progress' from unequal to more equal relationships?
Willmott and Young argued that changes in family life begin among the _____ class and spread downwards to the working class.
The concept of _____ describes a socially constructed stage of life between childhood and adulthood, whose length and meaning vary across societies.
Match each sociologist/concept to their argument about changing family relationships:
right: The symmetrical family represents a positive march of progress towards greater equality
The domestic division of labour remains unequal; greater female participation in work creates a double shift
The privatisation of family life serves capitalism by tying families to home-centred consumption

glossary_terms.definition: Willmott and Young's term for a modern family form in which partners share domestic tasks and leisure relatively equally, though roles are not identical.
Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread down to the working class over time.
A socially constructed stage of life between childhood and adulthood, characterised by physical maturation and changing social expectations; its length and meaning vary across societies.
A marriage in which families play a significant role in identifying and vetting potential partners, but the individuals involved give their informed consent.
Willmott and Young's term for a home-centred lifestyle in which family life is focused inward on the domestic sphere, with leisure and social life concentrated within the household.
Referring to relationships or patterns that span two or more generations within a family, such as grandparent–parent–child relationships.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Willmott and Young mean by the 'symmetrical family'?
flashcard_questions.a: A modern family in which both partners share domestic tasks and leisure relatively equally, though not identically.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote The Symmetrical Family and in what year?
What is the principle of stratified diffusion?
flashcard_questions.a: Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread to the working class.
Willmott and Young's term for a home-centred lifestyle in which family life is focused inward on the domestic sphere.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Oakley challenge Willmott and Young's 'march of progress' claim?
flashcard_questions.a: She showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and criticised their low threshold for male participation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is adolescence as a sociological concept?
flashcard_questions.a: A socially constructed life stage between childhood and adulthood whose length and meaning vary across societies.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do feminist sociologists argue that care of elderly relatives is a gendered issue?
flashcard_questions.a: Caring responsibilities fall disproportionately on women, adding to their domestic burden alongside paid work.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes an arranged marriage from a forced marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: In an arranged marriage individuals give their informed consent; forced marriage is coercive and illegal in the UK.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Marxist critique say about Willmott and Young's symmetrical family?
flashcard_questions.a: Privatised home-centred life ties families to consumption patterns that benefit capitalism rather than representing genuine freedom.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the role of the pre-industrial family in economic terms?
flashcard_questions.a: It was primarily a unit of economic production, with family members of all ages contributing to agriculture or craft work.

hero_image_caption: Sociologists trace how family relationships have changed from pre-industrial production units to contemporary domestic partnerships.
